data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The preference smuggles induction back in because acting on corroboration necessarily assumes the uniformity of nature or the stability of laws, which Popper explicitly rejected; the only defensible stance is a radical skepticism where preference is merely a psychological habit with no rational justification.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If a non-inductive basis for action can be found, such as a purely conventional or decision-theoretic rule that does not rely on nature's uniformity.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If 'preference' is redefined strictly as 'selection for further testing' rather than 'selection for application'.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Any decision to act on a theory (e.g., build a bridge using Newtonian physics) presupposes that the future will resemble the past regarding that theory's validity. This is the definition of induction. Popper's attempt to label this 'pragmatic' or 'evolutionary' is semantic sleight of hand. If corroboration gives no reason to believe a theory will work tomorrow, then preferring it is irrational unless one secretly assumes inductive regularity.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
